New Zealand Paper Gives Hawaiian Nark Free Ride On Prohibitionist Propaganda
"Singapore an example that New Zealand and the United States could follow."

(Marijuananews note: There are four interesting points here.

First, a US nark is invited to pitch really extreme reefer madness in New Zealand. This gives new meaning to the cliché about the long arm of the law.

Second, the police are heavily involved in the maintenance of the ideology of marijuana prohibition. And to be blunt, they have little regard for the truth.
See

Third, he gets a free ride from this New Zealand paper. No questions about even his most extreme positions.

Fourth, he is a native Hawaiian, who was apparently speaking to and about the indigenous New Zealanders, the Maori’s, who make up about 12 percent of the 3,500,000 population.

He is lying to get the Maori leaders to pressure the Anglo majority to keep the police power over the Maori’s, who are presumed incapable of controlling themselves. This is a position taken by most minority leaders in DEAland, that their people can’t handle freedom.

If a white person says this sort of thing, it would immediately -- and rightly -- be denounced as racist. When a member of the minority leadership opposes individual freedom for members of the minority, "enlightened" whites can never object.)

January 21, 1999

From the Dominion
New Zealand
http://www.inl.co.nz/wnl/dominion/index.html
letters@dominion.co.nz
By JONATHAN MILNE

HAWAIIAN drug enforcement officer has criticised the New Zealand police’s "soft and lazy" stance in dealing with cannabis problems.

See

He said New Zealand politicians appeared to be seriously considering loosening the law on cannabis use and possession, and police were half-hearted about enforcing the law.

"I was appalled. In America, I know of no law enforcement agency that would ever succumb to legalisation in any form," he said.

(Marijuananews note: Interesting terminology and perspective. If the people break free, then their police masters are succumbing. This illustrates the degree to which marijuana prohibition is an essential part of the police ideology. Of course, not all police really believe this, but most feel constrained to go along.)

"Federal, state and municipal law enforcement agencies continue to take a fervent stand against any form of legalisation - any form ... at all."

See

He said cannabis was a particular problem among indigenous peoples such as native Hawaiians and Maoris, who were generally in a lower socioeconomic group.

The high proportion of people of indigenous heritage in prisons - 80 per cent in Hawaii and 50 per cent in New Zealand - was a direct result of drug use, he said.

(Marijuananews note: Most of these arrests are from alcohol related crimes. Prohibition creates most of the rest. Therefore, marijuana must remain illegal??)

"It’s from drug use that people are led to a number of other crimes, from burglaries to homicide."

Despite Hawaii’s and New Zealand’s relative isolation as island states, he said customs services were unable to stop the influx of hard drugs. He said cannabis was a drug that nations could never afford to legalise,
and enforcement needed to take the forefront, along with education.
See

He pointed to Singapore, with its tough anti-drug laws, as an example that New Zealand and the United States could follow.
See
Drug Testing In Singapore and Oklahoma – 2 Stories
– "A JOBLESS man who defied narcotics officers by peeing in his trousers,   rather than provide a urine sample has been sentenced to six years’ jail and three strokes of the cane."  Where We Are Going

"The people of New Zealand cannot allow, in any way, shape or form, the legalisation of a drug that’s been proven scientifically to not only be harmful to anyone who uses it, but [also] has absolutely no health benefit to users."
See
Lester Grinspoon Attends Two Conferences On Medical Marijuana In Germany
And Our Drug Czar Says that Medical Marijuana Is A Hoax To Legalize Drugs – Analysis Plus 2 Articles

Through a spokeswoman, Government duty minister Bill English said cannabis was a controlled drug and it was illegal to possess it.
See

"The Government has not signalled any intention to change that, but there’s a legitimate debate about the best way to avoid the harm it can do," he said.

See
New Zealand Paper Reports "Marijuana use may be inching towards decriminalisation."

Mr Kaonohi said he visited medical clinics in Waikato, where children and adults exhibited physical problems and sickness stemming from marijuana use.

A lax attitude to drug enforcement in Hawaii five or six years ago had resulted in problems in the schools and social services, with children and babies impaired by their parents’ drug use, he said. More than 1000 "drug babies" were born each year in Hawaii - a problem that New Zealand could also face.
